stem: Match each type expression with the type it simplifies to.
explanation: Think of types as sets of values. `unknown` is the set of everything, so it absorbs any union and disappears from any intersection. `never` is the empty set, so it disappears from unions and absorbs intersections. These identities explain why `never` vanishes from mapped or conditional results.

options.why: A `const` keeps the union of literals produced by the conditional.
The union of inferred literals is a widening literal type, so it widens when copied into a `let`.
Only explicitly annotated literal types resist widening; these were inferred.
TypeScript cannot know which branch runs, so it keeps both possibilities.

explanation: Each branch produces a widening literal type, and the `const` keeps the union `"a" | "b"`. Copying it into a mutable `let` widens every member, giving `string`. To keep the union in `y`, annotate it, or annotate `x` with `"a" | "b"` explicitly so the literals are non-widening.
reference: TypeScript PR #10676: Always use literal types

stem: Given `const t: [number, string] = [1, 'a'];`, which statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: `t.push(2);` compiles, even though it breaks the tuple's length
options.why: Mutable tuple types still inherit `push` from `Array`, a known soundness gap.

options.text: `t[2];` is a compile error, because the tuple has no element at index 2
options.why: Index access beyond a fixed tuple's length is checked.

options.text: The type of `t.length` is the literal `2`
options.why: Fixed-length tuples have a literal length type.

options.text: `t.push(2);` is a compile error, because tuples are fixed length
options.why: Only `readonly` tuples drop `push`; mutable tuples allow it.
That is true for arrays and for tuples with rest elements, but not for this fixed tuple.

options.text: `t[0] = 'x';` compiles, because tuple elements can be any union member
options.why: Each position keeps its own type, so index 0 must be a number.

explanation: Tuples are arrays with per-position types and a literal length, but mutable tuples still expose `push`, `pop` and `splice`, which can make the static type wrong at runtime. Declare tuples `readonly` (or create them `as const`) when their shape must not change.

options.why: A `const` symbol has a `unique symbol` type, so it becomes a named property key.

options.text: `obj` is `{ [k]: number }` and `obj2` is `{ [x: symbol]: number }`
options.why: Only a `unique symbol` can be a known property key; a plain `symbol` key becomes an index signature.

options.text: Both are `{ [k]: number }`, because the two symbols have the same description
options.why: Descriptions do not matter; every `Symbol()` call creates a distinct value.

options.text: `obj` is `{}` and `obj2` is `{}`, because symbol keys are not typed
options.why: TypeScript tracks symbol-keyed properties; it does not drop them.

explanation: `const k = Symbol()` has type `typeof k`, a `unique symbol`, so `{ [k]: 1 }` gets a real, named property `[k]`. A `let` symbol has the general `symbol` type, so TypeScript can only describe the object with a symbol index signature. This is why well-known keys are declared with `const` (or `unique symbol` in `.d.ts` files).

options.why: That swaps them: `keyof typeof` gives the member names, and the template gives the values.
`typeof Color` is the enum object, whose keys are the names; the template literal turns members into their string values.

options.text: `K` is the methods of `String`, and `V` is `string`
options.why: That is what `keyof Color` (without `typeof`) gives, because `Color` the type is a string subtype.

options.text: Both are `Color`, because enum types cannot be converted to string unions
options.why: Template literal types can interpolate enum types, producing a union of their values.

explanation: Two different things are called `Color`: the type (the union of members) and the runtime object. `keyof typeof Color` reads the keys of the object, giving the member names. `${Color}` interpolates each member's value, giving the union of string values, which is handy for accepting plain strings at an API boundary. `keyof Color` is a classic mistake: it gives the keys of `String`.
